In summary, our research is concerned with

the short-term effects of plants on bacterial communities and PAH degradation in an aged-contaminated field soil, with a focus on the link between plant-mediated changes in the microbiome and the availability of carbon sources.
the short-term effect of ryegrass on bacterial communities and potential phenanthrene-degrading bacteria in an aged-contaminated site.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
plants can alter the rhizosphere microbiome in a way that is not necessarily linked to the dissipation of PAHs.
plants induced a shift in the rhizospheric microbiome, but this did not translate into a significant effect on the abundance or the activity of phenanthrene degrading genes.
plants induced a short-term shift in the composition of rhizospherical communities and the potential for PAH biodegradation, which might influence the long-term fate of PAHs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
plants can rapidly alter the composition and activity of resident and active bacterial community, and that these changes are related to the quality of carbon sources and phenanthrene degradation.
plants have the ability to modify the rhizosphere microbiome, and the effects on the active microbial community might be more profound than those on resident community.

plants can strongly influence the assembly of resident and active bacterial community in aged-contaminanted soil by providing a cocktail of labial DOC and by changing the identity of potential PAH-degraders, but this influence might be transient and not necessarily translate into a higher dissipation of phenathrene on the long-term.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plants can strongly affect the composition and activity of the soil microbiome, but this influence is highly variable and may depend on plant species.
the rhizosphere can rapidly modify the composition of the active microbiome in an aged-contaminated and PAH-polluted soil.

plant-induced rhizosphere effect is a complex phenomenon that involves the activity of multiple microbial groups and that is strongly linked to soil contamination history and the composition of the carbon pool.
